findings.title: Separate proposed deployments, rejected changes and actual damage

evidence.detail: Metrics list deployment count and unsafe changes; the latter includes safety-gate rejection and executed harm.

Embedded data and comparison renderer count every action=deploy as a deployment, even when the result is safety-gate rejection. Across A2, 5 attempted deployments comprise 3 applied actions and 2 rejections.
A1 has 32 deployment attempts: 27 applied and 5 rejected. Its 9 unsafe flags mix rejection and applied harmful action.
The assessment already recommends separating harmful proposals, rejected unsafe actions and actual damage.

findings.impact: A rejected proposal did not modify the deployment. Labels currently conflate policy risk with effective system changes, and unsafe_changes combines several events with different operational meaning. Healthy-tick primary results remain correct.
findings.recommendation: Preserve historical fields; add versioned derived deployment_attempts, rejected_unsafe_attempts, applied_actions, effective_state_changes and harmful_applied_changes. Keep all six customer ticks as the common primary denominator.
findings.status: acknowledged in assessment; derived metric labels not yet corrected

findings.title: The qualification gate admits a policy that preserves healthy systems by failing to repair damaged ones

evidence.detail: Qualification requires complete/valid execution and no false_alarm regression, but no recovery competence in an uncorrupted damaged control.
A2 is accurately reported as passing this narrow gate.
Eight of nine damaged-case episodes end unhealthy; three healthy controls stay healthy. Only reset/migrated_data recovers.
The missing matched damaged, no-misleading-memory baseline is explicitly required for the next study.

findings.impact: Operationally valid answers and healthy-system restraint do not establish the competence needed to interpret a memory-repair contrast. A wait-dominated policy passes while recovering almost nothing. This is a limitation of the originally chosen gate, not a reason to relabel its observed pass as failure.
findings.recommendation: Keep the historical gate result unchanged, stop escalation, and require both clean damaged-task recovery and healthy-system preservation in the next prespecified gate. Separate model/schema validity, competence, scientific contrast and process compliance.
findings.status: accurately acknowledged; no further launches recommended

findings.title: Standalone images omit the run identity required by their own visualization specification

evidence.detail: Requires case, seed, arm, source hash and backend in every view.
Image title says anthropic but does not identify solo architecture, seed 9101, amendment or source hash.
Same pixels as a2 final_frame despite different seed ranges/source versions; no embedded source/seed label allows standalone identification.

findings.impact: Separate final-frame exports can lose their provenance when shared outside the folder. The HTML views do expose backend/source and selectors, and the comparison chart gives appropriate one-episode caveats.
findings.recommendation: Add a compact footer with run/architecture, selected seed or aggregation rule, source prefix and scripted/native label; use stepped state timelines for discrete ticks and distinguish overlapping arms without adding decorative motion.

updated_conclusions: The scenario redesign is materially stronger than the older immune ledger instrument: relational compatibility/data/feature constraints, multiple feasible repairs, observed revision metadata, a healthy false-alarm control and a solo comparator reduce prior structural advantages and expose actual model errors.

Native evidence now exists for this new scenario instrument: 28 assigned/recorded episodes across team A1/A2 and solo A1. The previous EP review conclusion about scripted v3 ledger evidence must not be generalized to say the entire project lacks native evidence.

The updated prose responsibly distinguishes execution success, narrow qualification and scientific capability. A1 damages healthy controls. A2 preserves those controls but fails to recover in eight of nine damaged episodes. Solo recovers all three damaged cases but harms the healthy control. No robust immunity or causal benefit of reviewers/memory filtering is established.

The main tables and comparison figure reconcile exactly with saved action traces. The 384 unique scripted episodes show feasibility under a deterministic visible-contract policy, not broad task diversity or model effectiveness.

Source names/suffixes are correctly described as presentation variants; four cases with one native sample per cell cannot support population-level or pooled significance claims. Team/solo order and model stochasticity prevent attributing observed differences solely to reviewers.

All 38 frozen file hashes match. Six replays contain 604 physical episode copies; scenario-engineering duplicates scenario-engineering-a1. There are 412 unique episodes and 2472 unique recorded ticks, including 28 native episodes and 168 native commander ticks.

Native cost addition is correct: .169049+.221422+.050788=.441259 and summary calls total 240. Provider usage/cost authenticity and reviewer-call completeness cannot be independently checked without the call ledger.
